exam: IISER Aptitude Test (IAT) 2027 preparation — provisional 2026-pattern pilot
title: IAT New Test 2
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Fresh original AI-assisted authorship to the 25-test plan and revised IAT instructions; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A seed plant bears ovules exposed on cone scales and does not enclose its mature seeds in a fruit. Which group fits both observations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gymnosperms.
Why: An exposed ovule can mature into a naked seed. Gymnosperms bear seeds without the enclosing ovary that later becomes a fruit; the two observations therefore reinforce the same identification.
Why not the others: (B) Angiosperm ovules are inside an ovary and their seeds are enclosed in fruit. (C) Bryophytes reproduce by spores rather than seeds. (D) Pteridophytes also lack seeds and produce spores.
Key point: Locate the ovule before fertilisation and the seed after it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: In a flower, sepals, petals and stamens appear above an ovary to which the floral tube is fused. Which pair describes it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Inferior ovary; epigynous.
Why: Fusion of the floral tube around the ovary puts the apparent insertion of the other whorls above it. That relative position defines an inferior ovary and an epigynous flower, regardless of the flower's size.
Why not the others: (A) Hypogynous whorls arise below a superior ovary. (C) A perigynous cup surrounds but does not fuse to a superior ovary in this way. (D) Combines incompatible relative positions.
Key point: Judge ovary position from the insertion and fusion of floral parts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure compares three cell fractions after independent repeat isolation. Which fraction most strongly supports a peroxisome identification, using both positive and negative markers?
options: A) Fraction P, because chlorophyll is abundant
B) Fraction Q, because ribosomal RNA is abundant
C) Fraction R, because catalase is enriched while chlorophyll and ribosomal RNA are low
D) All three equally, because each contains protein
questions.image_alt: Bar chart: P has high chlorophyll and low catalase; Q has high ribosomal RNA and low catalase; R has high catalase and low chlorophyll and ribosomal RNA; repeated preparations show the same pattern.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Fraction R.
Why: The figure shows strong catalase enrichment specifically in R, with little chlorophyll or ribosomal RNA. Catalase supports a peroxisome-rich preparation, while the low negative markers argue against chloroplast or ribosome contamination. Repeated isolation reduces the chance of a single separation accident.
Why not the others: (A) P's chlorophyll instead points to plastid material. (B) Q's RNA points to ribosome-rich material. (D) Protein occurs in many compartments and cannot identify an organelle.
Key point: Combine a positive marker with contamination controls.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure plots net photosynthesis against light at two fixed CO₂ concentrations and constant temperature. Which conclusion is best supported over the measured range?
options: A) Extra light always lowers net photosynthesis
B) High CO₂ prevents any light response
C) The two curves show that temperature changed
D) The low-CO₂ curve plateaus sooner, while high CO₂ permits a larger response to light
questions.image_alt: Net photosynthetic rate versus light intensity: the low-CO₂ curve rises then plateaus near 3 units; the high-CO₂ curve rises to about 9 units at higher light, at constant temperature.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Low CO₂ limits the light response sooner.
Why: At high light, the low-CO₂ trace is nearly flat while the high-CO₂ trace continues rising. Increasing light therefore adds little when carbon supply is limiting, but increases carbon fixation when CO₂ is less restrictive. The comparison holds temperature fixed.
Why not the others: (A) Neither curve decreases over the shown interval. (B) The high-CO₂ curve responds strongly to light. (C) Temperature was controlled, so the difference cannot be assigned to it.
Key point: Interpret paired interventions rather than naming a limiting factor from one curve.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At rest, heart rate is 60 min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 80 mL. During exercise, heart rate becomes 100 min⁻¹ while cardiac output rises by 25%. What is the new stroke volume?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 60 mL.
Given: Initial output is 60×80=4800 mL/min.
Formula/Principle: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Step 1: New output=1.25×4800=6000 mL/min.
Step 2: New stroke volume=6000/100=60 mL per beat.
Why: The output increases less proportionally than the rate, so the volume per beat must fall in this stipulated measurement.
Why not the others: (B) assumes unchanged stroke volume; (C) treats the new rate as volume; (D) doubles the correct value.
Key point: Calculate output before solving for a changed component.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A species has 2n=12. One homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I of a male meiocyte; meiosis II is normal. Each of the four sperm is considered for fertilisation with a normal egg. Which zygote chromosome counts can result?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 11 and 13.
Given: Normal gametes have n=6. The affected meiosis-I daughters receive both homologues or neither.
Formula/Principle: Normal meiosis II separates sisters without correcting the unequal homologues.
Step 1: The four sperm therefore have n+1=7 or n−1=5 chromosomes.
Step 2: Each normal egg contributes six, yielding 13 or 11.
Why: The error happened before the reductional division completed, so none of this meiocyte's products has the normal count.
Why not the others: (A) ignores nondisjunction; (C) counts two extra or missing homologues per gamete; (D) wrongly leaves one daughter normal.
Key point: Track homologues and sister chromatids in their respective divisions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Crossing two pure lines produces F₁ petals with distinct red and white patches; assays detect both parental pigment types. Which inheritance pattern best fits the observations?
options: B) Incomplete dominance producing a new pink pigment
C) Codominance of the two pigment traits
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Codominance.
Why: Both parental traits are visibly represented in the same F₁ rather than one masking the other. Detecting both pigment types supports simultaneous expression, not an intermediate pigment.
Why not the others: (A) Would hide white expression. (B) Predicts an intermediate blended phenotype rather than separate patches. (D) Nothing about the cross associates the trait with sex.
Key point: Distinguish coexistence of parental phenotypes from an intermediate one.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Equal doses of one antigen are given 40 days apart. Antibody rises slowly after the first dose but rapidly and much more after the second. Which mechanism explains the change without assuming a higher second dose?
options: A) The second injection bypasses antigen recognition
B) All innate immune cells become antigen-specific antibodies
C) The antigen becomes a different molecule after 40 days
D) Memory lymphocytes formed after first exposure respond faster on re-exposure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Immunological memory.
Why: Initial exposure activates antigen-specific lymphocytes and leaves memory cells after the first response contracts. Those cells are already selected for the same antigen, so the second exposure has a shorter lag and larger response at equal dose.
Why not the others: (A) Antigen recognition is still necessary. (B) Innate cells do not themselves turn into antibodies. (C) The experiment holds antigen identity fixed.
Key point: Compare response timing under a controlled repeat exposure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A vector and insert are cut with the same restriction enzyme to produce complementary overhangs. A second vector has blunt ends. All ends have the groups required by ligase. What advantage is specific to the first vector–insert pair?
options: A) Complementary overhangs can anneal and align ends before covalent ligation
B) Ligase acts only on overhangs and never on blunt ends
C) Complementary ends ensure a single insert orientation in every case
D) Cutting makes both DNA fragments single-stranded throughout
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Alignment by base pairing.
Why: Complementary short overhangs transiently anneal, increasing the chance that the vector and insert ends remain together for ligase to seal the backbone. This is a pairing advantage, not an absolute chemical requirement of ligase.
Why not the others: (B) Blunt ends can also be ligated. (C) Identical compatible ends can permit either orientation. (D) Only the overhang region is single-stranded.
Key point: Separate cohesive-end annealing from phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At equal intervals, a closed population is counted as 50, 90, 140, 180, 200 and 205; food supply is fixed and counts are accurate. Which interpretation fits the changing increments?
options: A) Exponential growth at a fixed per-capita rate
B) Growth slows as limiting resources become important
C) The population must have declined between every count
D) Immigration alone explains the final plateau
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Resource-limited growth.
Why: Increments rise at first but fall sharply near the last counts, even though the population remains positive and growing. With fixed food and no migration, density-dependent limitation is a coherent explanation for approaching a carrying level. The counts alone do not establish its exact value.
Why not the others: (A) Fixed exponential growth would not flatten this way. (C) Every recorded count rises. (D) Migration was excluded.
Key point: Compare successive increments, not just population sizes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An unaffected person has an affected sibling with an autosomal recessive disorder; both parents are unaffected. The person's unaffected partner has one confirmed carrier parent and one confirmed non-carrier parent. Under complete penetrance and independent families, what is their first child's affected risk?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/12.
Given: The affected sibling establishes carrier parents in the first family.
Formula/Principle: Condition on the person's unaffected status, then multiply independent carrier and transmission probabilities.
Step 1: Among unaffected children of Aa×Aa, two of three genotype classes are carriers: 2/3.
Step 2: Partner carrier probability from Aa×AA is 1/2; two carriers have an affected child with probability 1/4. Product=(2/3)(1/2)(1/4)=1/12.
Why: The condition of being unaffected removes the aa child from the first denominator.
Why not the others: (A) uses 1/3 carrier risk; (B) treats carrier status as certain; (D) omits the 1/4 child factor.
Key point: Recondition a pedigree probability when phenotype is known.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA coding region reads AUG | GAA | UCC | GCU | UAA. A single U is inserted immediately before the first base of the second codon, with translation still starting at AUG. What follows without consulting a codon chart?
options: A) Only one amino acid can change
B) Codon boundaries after AUG shift and several downstream amino acids may change
C) The start codon must disappear
D) Every codon after insertion remains unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Downstream frame shift.
Why: The ribosome reads consecutive, non-overlapping groups of three bases from the same initiation point. Adding one base after AUG changes which bases form every subsequent triplet until translation stops; even the location of a stop codon can change.
Why not the others: (A) Assumes the insertion replaced only one whole codon. (C) AUG lies before the insertion. (D) Triplet grouping cannot remain the same after a one-base insertion.
Key point: Track reading positions, not just the inserted letter.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A freely filtered solute has plasma concentration 1 mg/mL and filtration rate 100 mL/min. Urine flows at 1 mL/min with solute concentration 10 mg/mL. With no tubular secretion, what fraction of the filtered solute is reabsorbed?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 90%.
Given: Filtered load=100 mL/min×1 mg/mL=100 mg/min; excretion=1 mL/min×10 mg/mL=10 mg/min.
Formula/Principle: Reabsorbed load=filtered load−excreted load when secretion is absent.
Step 1: Reabsorbed=90 mg/min.
Step 2: Fraction=90/100=0.90.
Why: Concentrations alone cannot be compared because plasma filtration and urine flows differ.
Why not the others: (A) confuses urine flow with fraction; (B) is excreted fraction; (C) ignores loads; none gives 90%.
Key point: Convert concentrations to rates before subtracting.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A drug prevents spindle microtubules from attaching to kinetochores but leaves DNA replication intact. Cells accumulate with condensed chromosomes and seldom separate chromatids. Which immediate process is blocked?
options: A) DNA replication in S phase
B) Nuclear envelope breakdown before spindle formation
C) Anaphase separation of sister chromatids
D) Cytoplasmic translation of spindle proteins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chromatid separation.
Why: Unattached kinetochores fail the spindle-attachment checkpoint, preventing the coordinated onset of anaphase. Chromosomes can condense, yet sisters cannot segregate reliably to opposite poles. DNA replication has already occurred under the stated condition.
Why not the others: (A) Is expressly unaffected. (B) Condensed mitotic cells have reached a later stage. (D) Protein synthesis is not the specified inhibited event.
Key point: An attachment checkpoint links spindle status to chromatid separation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two C₃ leaves are held at identical light, temperature and stomatal conductance. Leaf Q has higher O₂ and lower CO₂ around Rubisco than leaf P. What change is expected in Q?
options: A) More oxygenation and photorespiratory carbon loss
B) No change because Rubisco binds only CO₂
C) More net fixation because O₂ is the carbon source
D) Elimination of the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) More photorespiration.
Why: Rubisco can catalyse both carboxylation and oxygenation. Raising O₂ relative to CO₂ shifts competition toward oxygenation, initiating photorespiratory reactions that consume resources and reduce net carbon gain under the controlled conditions. It need not stop all carboxylation.
Why not the others: (B) Ignores Rubisco's oxygenase activity. (C) O₂ supplies no carbon for fixation. (D) Reduced net gain is not complete abolition of the cycle.
Key point: Compare competing substrates at the same enzyme.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why is the H–N–H angle in NH₃ smaller than the H–C–H angle in CH₄?
options: A) Nitrogen forms four identical N–H bonds
B) Methane has a lone pair on carbon
C) Ammonia contains no tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement
D) A nitrogen lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair does
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion.
Why: Both centres have four electron domains, but NH₃ has three bond pairs and a lone pair. The more spatially demanding lone pair compresses the angles between N–H bonds below the ideal tetrahedral angle of CH₄.
Why not the others: (A) NH₃ has three N–H bonds. (B) Carbon has four bonds and no lone pair here. (C) Electron-domain geometry is approximately tetrahedral even though molecular geometry is pyramidal.
Key point: Distinguish electron-domain and molecular geometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows complexes P and Q with differently placed bromide and sulfate. Assume only freely dissociated counterions give immediate precipitates. Which observation distinguishes them on separate BaCl₂ and AgNO₃ tests?
options: A) P gives BaSO₄ and Q gives AgBr
B) P gives AgBr and Q gives BaSO₄
C) Both give each precipitate immediately
D) Neither gives an immediate precipitate
questions.image_alt: Complex P is [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4, with sulfate outside brackets; Q is [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br, with bromide outside brackets.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P gives BaSO₄, Q gives AgBr.
Why: Brackets in the figure delimit each coordination sphere. P has freely dissociated sulfate that Ba²⁺ removes as insoluble BaSO₄; Q has free bromide that Ag⁺ removes as AgBr. The coordinated ligands are not assumed to leave immediately.
Why not the others: (B) Reverses inner and outer sphere. (C) Treats every coordinated ligand as a counterion. (D) Ignores the actual counterions.
Key point: Read the brackets before predicting precipitation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hydrogen ionisation from an excited level
questions.question: Hydrogen has Eₙ=−13.6/n² eV. What minimum photon energy ionises an atom initially at n=2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3.4 eV.
Given: E₂=−13.6/4=−3.4 eV and E∞=0.
Formula/Principle: Absorption needs the energy difference final minus initial.
Step 1: ΔE=0−(−3.4)=+3.4 eV.
Why: The electron starts already above the ground state, so less than 13.6 eV is needed.
Why not the others: (A) Ground-state ionisation; (C) n=1→2 excitation; (D) Confuses the n=3 binding energy.
Key point: Set the continuum energy to zero before subtracting.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A primary carbocation lies next to a carbon bearing a hydride and two alkyl groups. If a 1,2-hydride shift precedes nucleophile capture, what chiefly favours that shift?
options: A) It necessarily creates an aromatic ring
B) It converts the positive charge into a negative charge
C) It relocates positive charge to a more substituted, more stable carbocation centre
D) It breaks all carbon–carbon bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A more stable carbocation.
Why: During a hydride shift, the C–H bonding pair migrates to the electron-deficient adjacent carbon. Positive charge then resides at the carbon that lost hydride, which is more substituted under the stated structure and stabilised by alkyl donation.
Why not the others: (A) No ring is specified. (B) Charge remains positive. (D) A hydride shift does not cleave all C–C bonds.
Key point: Track both the migrating electron pair and the new charge site.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Propene reacts with HBr first without and then with peroxide, with the radical pathway effective in the second experiment. What major products are expected respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2-bromopropane then 1-bromopropane.
Why: Ionic addition without peroxide proceeds through the more stable secondary carbocation, placing bromine on the middle carbon. The peroxide-initiated HBr radical chain favours the orientation that forms the more stable carbon radical and ultimately puts bromine on the terminal carbon.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the conditions. (B) Applies the radical result to both. (C) Omits the peroxide effect.
Key point: Choose the mechanism before choosing regioselectivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An optically active 2-bromobutane sample is divided. P undergoes clean backside SN2 substitution; Q is heated with a small alcoholic base and gives predominantly E2. Which combined outcome fits both mechanisms?
options: A) P inverts at C-2; Q mainly gives trans-but-2-ene among alkene isomers
B) P retains configuration; Q gives only but-1-ene
C) P racemises completely; Q gives only but-1-ene
D) P inverts; Q gives mainly butan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Inversion and a more substituted trans-favoured alkene.
Why: Backside displacement reverses the arrangement at the reacting stereocentre. E2 removes a β hydrogen with departure of bromide; with a small base, but-2-ene is generally favoured over but-1-ene, and its trans form is more stable than cis. These are separate stereochemical and regioselective decisions.
Why not the others: (B) Gives retention and the less substituted alkene. (C) Assigns planar-intermediate racemisation to SN2. (D) Names a substitution alcohol rather than an E2 product.
Key point: Analyse each reaction condition independently.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Liquids X and Y each release gas with sodium metal. Only X gives the usual coloured complex with neutral FeCl₃. Which assignment is best supported?
options: B) X phenol; Y a simple aliphatic alcohol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X phenol, Y alcohol.
Why: Sodium reacts with acidic O–H groups in both alcohol and phenol, so that test alone does not distinguish them. A neutral ferric chloride colour is characteristic of the phenolic group in this qualitative comparison, selecting X as phenol.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the distinguishing observation. (C) Ether and alkane lack the O–H needed for the stated sodium response. (D) An alkane cannot explain X's tests.
Key point: Interpret the two tests together, not independently.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Isomers X and Y have formula C₃H₆O. X gives Tollens-positive and iodoform-negative results; Y gives the reverse. What are X and Y?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Propanal and propanone.
Why: Propanal is an aldehyde and reduces Tollens reagent but lacks the methyl ketone group for the iodoform reaction. Propanone has CH₃CO– and gives iodoform, but an ordinary ketone does not reduce Tollens reagent. Both match C₃H₆O.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the tests. (B) Propan-1-ol has formula C₃H₈O. (D) Propan-2-ol also has that different formula and does not fit X's Tollens result.
Key point: Check both functional-group tests and molecular formula.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In water, aniline is appreciably less basic than cyclohexylamine. Which explanation addresses electron-pair availability at nitrogen?
options: A) Aniline has no nitrogen lone pair
C) The aniline nitrogen has a different valence
D) Aniline's lone pair delocalises into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Resonance lowers lone-pair availability.
Why: The aniline lone pair overlaps with the aromatic π system, stabilising the unprotonated base. Cyclohexylamine lacks this conjugation, so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton under comparable aqueous conditions. Solvation can matter, but the proposed resonance distinction is the central structural reason.
Why not the others: (A) The lone pair exists. (B) Cyclohexylamine is an amine. (C) Both nitrogens have ordinary amine valence.
Key point: Compare conjugation of the free base when assessing basicity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At fixed temperature, 0.020 mol glucose and 0.030 mol urea make 1.00 L ideal solution. Both are nonelectrolytes. What is its osmotic pressure divided by that of 0.020 M glucose at the same temperature?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.5.
Given: Total dissolved particle concentration is (0.020+0.030)/1.00=0.050 M.
Formula/Principle: Ideal osmotic pressure π=CRT for nonelectrolytes.
Step 1: Temperature and R cancel in the ratio.
Step 2: πmixture/πglucose=0.050/0.020=2.5.
Why: Each dissolved molecule contributes a particle; no ionisation factor is needed.
Why not the others: (B) Counts only urea relative to glucose; (C) reverses the ratio; (D) adds an unjustified dissociation factor.
Key point: Sum particle molarities, not solute identities.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Ag/Ag⁺ half-cells at 298 K contain 0.010 M and 1.0 M Ag⁺. With ideal solutions and negligible junction potential, use 0.059 V for 2.303RT/F. Which electrode is negative, and what emf results before appreciable composition change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The dilute electrode; +0.118 V.
Given: Silver reduction potential increases with [Ag⁺].
Formula/Principle: E=E°+0.059 log[Ag⁺] for Ag⁺+e⁻→Ag; Ecell=Ecathode−Eanode.
Step 1: Concentrated side is the cathode; dilute side oxidises and is negative.
Step 2: Ecell=0.059 log(1.0/0.010)=0.118 V.
Why: Oxidation on the dilute side tends to replenish Ag⁺ and diminish the concentration difference.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses polarity; (C) counts only one decade; (D) reverses polarity and emf sign.
Key point: Determine electrode roles before evaluating logarithms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure plots initial rates for trials 1–3 while one concentration is doubled at a time. Which empirical rate law follows?
questions.image_alt: Three trial bars show rate 2, 4 and 16 in units of 10^-3 M/s; concentration labels are trial 1 A=0.10,B=0.10 M; trial 2 A=0.20,B=0.10 M; trial 3 A=0.20,B=0.20 M.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) k[A][B]².
Given: Trial 1→2 doubles A alone and rate 2→4; trial 2→3 doubles B alone and rate 4→16.
Formula/Principle: At fixed other reactants, a doubling changes rate by 2 raised to that reactant's order.
Step 1: A factor 2 implies first order in A.
Step 2: B factor 4 implies second order in B.
Why: The controlled comparisons isolate one variable at a time, so a combined trial 1→3 ratio would obscure the separate exponents.
Why not the others: (A) swaps orders; (B) underpredicts trial 3; (D) overpredicts trial 2.
Key point: Read the trial labels as well as bar heights.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: On the same mole basis, ΔH(A→B)=+40 kJ/mol and ΔH(B→C)=−75 kJ/mol. Find ΔH(C→A).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +35 kJ/mol.
Given: A→C is the sum of the two given paths.
Formula/Principle: Enthalpy is a state function; reversing a reaction reverses ΔH.
Step 1: ΔH(A→C)=40−75=−35 kJ/mol.
Step 2: Therefore C→A has +35 kJ/mol.
Why: Endpoint states, not the route, fix the net enthalpy change.
Why not the others: (A) adds magnitudes then reverses; (B) forgets reversal; (C) adds magnitudes with wrong sign.
Key point: Draw the directed path before combining changes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 20.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. At 30.0 mL added, find pH at 25 °C, with additive volumes and Kw=10⁻¹⁴.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) pH 12.30.
Given: Acid=2.0 mmol; added base=3.0 mmol; final volume=50.0 mL.
Formula/Principle: Neutralise first; then pOH=−log[OH⁻], pH=14−pOH.
Step 1: Excess OH⁻=1.0 mmol/50.0 mL=0.020 M.
Step 2: pOH≈1.70 and pH≈12.30.
Why: Past equivalence, excess strong base controls pH rather than the neutral salt.
Why not the others: (B) Reports pOH; (C) assumes equivalence; (D) neglects excess-base dilution.
Key point: Count moles before taking a logarithm.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A transition-metal ion has exactly one unpaired electron. Under the spin-only approximation, what magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons is predicted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) √3 BM.
Given: Number of unpaired electrons n=1.
Formula/Principle: Spin-only μ=√[n(n+2)] BM.
Step 1: Substitute n=1: μ=√(1×3)=√3 BM.
Why: Spin-only counting depends on unpaired spins, not the total electron number or metal identity under this stipulated model.
Why not the others: (A) Omits the n+2 factor; (C) corresponds to n=2; (D) drops the square root.
Key point: Count unpaired electrons before evaluating the moment.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Distance from a centre to a tangent
questions.question: A circle with centre (3,4) touches the x-axis. Which ordinates occur where it intersects the positive y-axis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4±√7.
Given: Tangency to x-axis fixes radius 4.
Formula/Principle: Circle equation (x−3)²+(y−4)²=16.
Step 1: On the y-axis x=0, so (y−4)²=7.
Step 2: y=4±√7, and both values are positive.
Why: A vertical line through the y-axis meets this circle twice because the centre is only three units from it.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) each omit one intersection; (D) incorrectly compares radius with the centre's horizontal distance.
Key point: Check both square-root branches against the stated ray.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: An ellipse centred at the origin has major axis along x, focus (3,0) and right directrix x=9. What are its eccentricity and full minor-axis length?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/√3 and 6√2.
Given: c=3 and right directrix a/e=9.
Formula/Principle: c=ae, b²=a²−c².
Step 1: a/e=a²/c=9, so a²=27 and e=3/√27=1/√3.
Step 2: b²=27−9=18; full minor axis 2b=6√2.
Why: Both focus and directrix fix a rather than either datum alone.
Why not the others: (A) Uses 3/9 for e; (C) halves the axis length; (D) has e>1 and is not an ellipse.
Key point: Distinguish semiaxis b from axis length 2b.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real a is f(x)=x³−3ax²+3x strictly increasing for every real x?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −1≤a≤1.
Given: f′(x)=3[(x−a)²+1−a²].
Formula/Principle: A derivative nonnegative everywhere with only isolated zeros yields a strictly increasing polynomial.
Step 1: The minimum derivative is 3(1−a²), requiring |a|≤1.
Step 2: At ±1 it vanishes only at one point, so no interval is constant and endpoints remain valid.
Why: Requiring f′>0 everywhere would incorrectly discard boundary cases.
Why not the others: (A) Excludes valid endpoints; (B) and (D) include values beyond the permitted range.
Key point: Check whether isolated stationary points spoil strict monotonicity.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the total area between y=x² and y=2−x² over −2≤x≤2.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 8.
Given: Curves cross at x=±1, so the upper curve changes.
Formula/Principle: Area=∫₋₂²|2−2x²|dx, not a signed net integral.
Step 1: By even symmetry, area=2[∫₀¹(2−2x²)dx+∫₁²(2x²−2)dx].
Step 2: The two bracketed integrals are 4/3 and 8/3, giving 2×4=8.
Why: The outer lobes must be added after reversing their signed integrand.
Why not the others: (B) drops the symmetry factor; (C) counts only outer lobes; (D) results from using one sign over all intervals.
Key point: Split at every crossing when asked for area.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=x²−4x+5 with domain x≥2. Which inverse value f⁻¹(10) is valid under that domain restriction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5.
Given: f(x)=(x−2)²+1 and its domain is x≥2.
Formula/Principle: Inverse evaluation means solving f(x)=10 and retaining only inputs in the given domain.
Step 1: (x−2)²=9, so x=2±3, i.e. 5 or −1.
Step 2: Reject −1<2; f⁻¹(10)=5.
Why: The restricted parabola is one-to-one, whereas the unrestricted parabola is not.
Why not the others: (A) retains the prohibited branch; (B) selects that branch alone; (D) omits the translation and square-root relation.
Key point: Apply the domain restriction after solving the inverse equation.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For A with rows (1,2), (k,6), which k makes A singular?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3.
Given: A is a 2×2 matrix.
Formula/Principle: A square matrix is singular precisely when its determinant vanishes.
Step 1: det A=1×6−2k=6−2k.
Step 2: Setting it to zero gives k=3.
Why: At this value the second row is three times the first, so the columns cannot be independent.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) give determinants 2, −6 and −18, respectively, all nonzero.
Key point: Confirm a zero determinant by row dependence.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Factory A supplies 2/3 of parts with 1% defective; B supplies 1/3 with 4% defective. Given a defective part, what is the chance it came from B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/3.
Given: Defective shares are (2/3)(.01) from A and (1/3)(.04) from B.
Formula/Principle: Posterior share=source's joint defective probability divided by all defective probability.
Step 1: Contributions have ratio 2:4.
Step 2: B share=4/(2+4)=2/3.
Why: A's larger output does not cancel B's larger defect rate.
Why not the others: (B) uses the prior alone; (C) assumes equal contributions; (D) ignores source proportions.
Key point: Weight likelihoods by source frequency.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the constant term in (x²−1/x)⁶ for x≠0.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 15.
Given: Choosing k factors −1/x leaves x exponent 2(6−k)−k=12−3k.
Formula/Principle: Binomial term is C(6,k)(x²)^(6−k)(−1/x)^k.
Step 1: Set exponent zero: k=4.
Step 2: Coefficient=C(6,4)(−1)^4=15.
Why: The even selected index makes the sign positive.
Why not the others: (A) loses parity; (C) uses k=3; (D) makes both mistakes.
Key point: Solve the exponent condition before the coefficient.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Arithmetic progression from two partial sums
questions.question: An arithmetic progression has S₅=25 and S₁₀=100. What is its twentieth term?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 39.
Given: Sₙ=n[2a+(n−1)d]/2.
Formula/Principle: Two sums determine initial term a and common difference d.
Step 1: S₅=25 gives a+2d=5; S₁₀=100 gives 2a+9d=20.
Step 2: Subtract twice the first relation: 5d=10, so d=2,a=1. Then a₂₀=a+19d=39.
Why: Using S₁₀−S₅ gives a five-term sum, not the twentieth term.
Why not the others: (A) confuses n and term; (B) is a₁₉; (C) is a₂₁.
Key point: Use sums to recover the underlying sequence.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Second-order radical limit from a first-order condition
questions.question: For real a, lim(x→0)[√(1+ax)−1]/x=3. Find lim(x→0)[√(1+ax)−1−3x]/x².
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −9/2.
Given: First limit equals a/2, hence a=6.
Formula/Principle: Expansion √(1+t)=1+t/2−t²/8+o(t²) near zero.
Step 1: √(1+6x)=1+3x−36x²/8+o(x²).
Step 2: Divide the residual by x² to get −9/2.
Why: The subtraction removes the first-order term; retaining only that term yields a false zero.
Why not the others: (A) loses the negative sign; (B) and (C) omit the square of a.
Key point: Use the first limit to fix the parameter before the second-order limit.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: L₁: r=(1,0,0)+t(1,1,0); L₂: r=(0,0,2)+s(0,1,1). Find their shortest distance.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/√3.
Given: Direction vectors u=(1,1,0), v=(0,1,1); displacement from L₁ to L₂ is w=(−1,0,2).
Formula/Principle: For nonparallel skew lines, distance=|w·(u×v)|/|u×v|.
Step 1: u×v=(1,−1,1), magnitude √3.
Step 2: w·(u×v)=−1+2=1; distance=1/√3.
Why: Only the component of separation along the common normal cannot be removed by moving along either line.
Why not the others: (A) omits normalisation; (B) uses vertical displacement; (C) multiplies instead of dividing by √3.
Key point: Project separation onto the unit common normal.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Six distinct people A–F sit at a round table, rotations identical but reflections distinct. How many arrangements have A not beside B and C not beside D?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 48.
Given: Total circular arrangements (6−1)!=120.
Formula/Principle: Inclusion-exclusion over adjacency AB and CD.
Step 1: Each adjacent pair as a block gives 2(5−1)!=48 arrangements.
Step 2: Both pairs as blocks give 2²(4−1)!=24.
Step 3: Neither=120−48−48+24=48.
Why: The overlap must be restored after subtracting the two forbidden sets.
Why not the others: (A) counts the overlap; (C) subtracts only one event; (D) omits the overlap correction.
Key point: Count rotations once at every block stage.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For z=x+iy, impose |z−(2+i)|=|z−(−2+i)| and |z−i|=3. Which pair of z values satisfies both?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4i and −2i.
Given: Equal distance from (2,1) and (−2,1) puts the point on their perpendicular bisector.
Formula/Principle: First locus x=0; second circle x²+(y−1)²=9.
Step 1: Substitute x=0 to obtain y−1=±3.
Step 2: y=4 or −2, hence z=4i or −2i.
Why: Both constraints must hold; the first locus alone is a whole line.
Why not the others: (B) uses circle centred at origin; (C) violates x=0; (D) treats the imaginary coordinate as real.
Key point: Intersect loci geometrically before solving algebraically.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: First-order linear equation with initial value
questions.question: Solve y′+2y=e^(−x), y(0)=0. What is y(ln 2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/4.
Given: Integrating factor e^(2x).
Formula/Principle: (e^(2x)y)′=e^x.
Step 1: Integrate: e^(2x)y=e^x+C; y(0)=0 gives C=−1.
Step 2: y=e^(−x)−e^(−2x); at ln 2, y=1/2−1/4=1/4.
Why: The integrating factor converts the linked y′ and y terms into one product derivative.
Why not the others: (A) drops the homogeneous term; (C) adds instead of subtracts; (D) ignores the initial condition.
Key point: Check the constant with the initial value before evaluation.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many distinct solutions of sin(2x)=cos x lie in 0≤x<2π?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.
Given: sin2x=2sin x cos x.
Formula/Principle: Factor the equation as cos x(2sin x−1)=0 without dividing by cos x.
Step 1: cos x=0 gives π/2 and 3π/2.
Step 2: sin x=1/2 gives π/6 and 5π/6, all in the half-open interval.
Why: Dividing by cos x would lose two valid solutions.
Why not the others: (A) counts only one factor; (B) misses a quadrant; (C) double-counts a boundary or extraneous point.
Key point: Preserve zero-factor branches before simplifying.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Masses 3m and m hang over a light frictionless pulley fixed to a lift accelerating upward at g. Relative to the lift, what is the magnitude of their acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) g.
Given: The lift's effective downward gravity is g+g=2g.
Formula/Principle: Atwood acceleration=(M−m)/(M+m) times effective gravity.
Step 1: Mass ratio=(3m−m)/(3m+m)=1/2.
Step 2: Relative acceleration=(1/2)(2g)=g.
Why: In the noninertial lift frame, the upward lift acceleration adds a downward pseudo acceleration.
Why not the others: (B) ignores lift motion; (C) ignores mass ratio; (D) incorrectly equates unequal tensions and weights.
Key point: Specify the frame before using an effective g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A force in the direction of motion has magnitude F(x)=2x N when x is in metres. How much work does it do from x=0 to x=3 m?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9 J.
Given: Force rises linearly from 0 to 6 N.
Formula/Principle: Work=∫F dx, the area under the force–displacement curve.
Step 1: ∫₀³2x dx=[x²]₀³=9 N·m.
Step 2: Convert N·m to 9 J.
Why: Using the final force for the whole interval overcounts the work because the force was smaller earlier.
Why not the others: (A) drops the coefficient; (B) uses an incorrect average force; (C) uses final force throughout.
Key point: Integrate when force changes with position.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Escape speed versus distance from centre
questions.question: Neglecting atmosphere and rotation, a planet's escape speed is v at radius R from its centre. What is escape speed at radius 4R?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) v/2.
Given: The same planet has mass M at both radii.
Formula/Principle: vesc=√(2GM/r).
Step 1: Ratio vesc(4R)/vesc(R)=√(R/4R).
Step 2: This is 1/2.
Why: Escape energy depends on gravitational potential GM/r, and speed is its square root.
Why not the others: (A) scales speed linearly with 1/r; (B) and (D) make speed rise with distance.
Key point: Distinguish inverse-radius energy from inverse-square-root speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A reversibly loaded material follows a straight stress–strain line from (0,0) to (2ε,2S), where ε and S are positive. What energy density is stored at strain 2ε?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2Sε.
Given: Stress increases linearly to 2S over strain range 2ε.
Formula/Principle: Reversible strain energy per volume is ∫stress d(strain), the triangular area.
Step 1: Area=(1/2)(2ε)(2S).
Step 2: The result is 2Sε, with pressure units J/m³.
Why: Each small strain increment stores its current stress times the increment, not the final stress for the entire path.
Why not the others: (A) halves the area twice; (C) adds an extra rectangle; (D) uses final stress over the whole range.
Key point: Read energy from the complete loading path.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Ice-water calorimetry with a phase change
questions.question: An insulated vessel mixes 100 g ice at 0 °C with 300 g water at 50 °C. Use cwater=4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Lfusion=336 J g⁻¹. Neglect vessel heat capacity. Find final temperature.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 17.5 °C.
Given: Hot water can release 300×4.2×50=63000 J by cooling to 0 °C; melting all ice needs 100×336=33600 J.
Formula/Principle: Test the phase-change threshold before balancing sensible heat.
Step 1: All ice melts, leaving 29400 J of heat.
Step 2: The 400 g resulting liquid warms by 29400/(400×4.2)=17.5 K.
Why: Temperature stays at 0 °C during melting; only excess energy raises the final temperature.
Why not the others: (B) overlooks available heat; (C) neglects latent heat; (D) heats the wrong water mass.
Key point: Resolve phase change before using a single temperature-balance equation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: RMS-speed ratio at a common temperature
questions.question: Two ideal gases at equal absolute temperature have molar masses in ratio 4:9. What is the ratio of their rms speeds in the same order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3:2.
Given: T is common; M₁:M₂=4:9.
Formula/Principle: vrms=√(3RT/M).
Step 1: v₁/v₂=√(M₂/M₁).
Step 2: √(9/4)=3/2.
Why: At equal mean translational kinetic energy, lighter molecules move faster.
Why not the others: (A) uses masses directly; (B) fails to invert; (C) inverts but omits square root.
Key point: RMS speed is inversely proportional to square root of molar mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Period of series and parallel springs
questions.question: Two identical springs of constant k support the same mass m, first in series and then in parallel. What is Tseries/Tparallel for small oscillations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: kseries=k/2, kparallel=2k.
Formula/Principle: T=2π√(m/keffective).
Step 1: Ratio=√(kparallel/kseries).
Step 2: √[(2k)/(k/2)]=√4=2.
Why: The series connection is softer and therefore oscillates more slowly.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the ratio; (B) changes only one spring configuration; (D) omits the square root.
Key point: Find equivalent stiffness before comparing periods.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy of disconnected series capacitors after dielectric insertion
questions.question: Capacitors C and 2C are in series with charge Q after disconnection from a source. A dielectric doubles only the first capacitance with no leakage. Find final/initial ratios of total stored energy and voltage on the modified element.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2/3 and 1/2.
Given: Both series capacitors retain charge Q; C changes to 2C.
Formula/Principle: Utotal=ΣQ²/(2Ci), Vmodified=Q/Cmodified.
Step 1: Ui=Q²/(2C)+Q²/(4C)=3Q²/(4C).
Step 2: Uf=Q²/(4C)+Q²/(4C)=Q²/(2C), so Uf/Ui=2/3.
Step 3: Voltage changes Q/C→Q/(2C), a factor 1/2.
Why: Source disconnection fixes charge, not voltage.
Why not the others: (A) reverses energy ratio; (C) reverses voltage ratio; (D) assumes fixed energy.
Key point: Identify the conserved electrical quantity first.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Magnetic force with two field components
questions.question: A positive charge q moves at speed v along +x in field B(ĵ+k̂), with B>0. Which magnetic-force vector acts on it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) qvB(k̂−ĵ).
Given: v=vî and magnetic field has equal +y and +z components.
Formula/Principle: F=q(v×B).
Step 1: î×ĵ=k̂, while î×k̂=−ĵ.
Step 2: Add component forces to obtain qvB(k̂−ĵ).
Why: The force is perpendicular to velocity and to the net field, not along either field component.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the cross-product order; (C) treats force as parallel to B; (D) ignores nonparallel motion.
Key point: Apply the right-hand rule separately to each component.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Potential change from a signed field graph
questions.question: The figure shows Eₓ as a function of x between 0 and 3a, with E₀,a>0. What is V(3a)−V(0)?
questions.image_alt: E_x is +2E0 from x=0 to a and −E0 from x=a to 3a, with horizontal constant segments and labelled axes.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Zero.
Given: The graph's positive rectangle has area 2E₀a; the negative rectangle has area −E₀(2a)=−2E₀a.
Formula/Principle: ΔV=−∫Eₓ dx, using signed area.
Step 1: The two signed field areas cancel.
Step 2: Therefore the negative of their sum is also zero.
Why: Field reverses direction but remains nonzero; equal opposite potential contributions can cancel.
Why not the others: (A) adds area magnitudes; (B) omits the second interval; (C) omits the first interval.
Key point: Retain signs and widths when reading an E–x graph.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A Wheatstone bridge has upper/lower left arms 2 Ω and 3 Ω and upper/lower right arms 4 Ω and R. An ideal galvanometer joins the midpoints. For zero galvanometer current, find R.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6 Ω.
Given: Corresponding upper/lower resistance ratios must match for midpoint potentials to agree.
Formula/Principle: Bridge balance: 2/3=4/R.
Step 1: Cross-multiply 2R=12.
Step 2: R=6 Ω.
Why: Zero galvanometer current means no potential difference between its terminals, independent of the galvanometer's resistance.
Why not the others: (A) uses reciprocal ratio; (B) copies the left lower arm; (D) incorrectly adds arm resistances.
Key point: Match like-position arm ratios.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Lens and plane mirror on a common axis
questions.question: The figure places an object 30 cm left of a converging lens of focal length 10 cm and a plane mirror 20 cm right of the lens. After reflection and a second lens passage, where is the final image? Use paraxial rays.
options: A) 15 cm left of the lens
B) 50/3 cm left of the lens
C) 25 cm right of the lens
D) 50/3 cm right of the lens
questions.image_alt: Object O lies 30 cm left of a converging lens marked f=10 cm; a plane mirror is 20 cm right of the lens, perpendicular to the optical axis. No image positions are drawn.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 50/3 cm left.
Given: Initial object distance 30 cm and lens-to-mirror distance 20 cm.
Formula/Principle: For each lens traversal 1/f=1/u+1/v; mirror images sit equally far behind a plane mirror.
Step 1: First image is v=15 cm right of lens, 5 cm in front of mirror.
Step 2: Mirror image is 5 cm behind it, 25 cm right of lens, now an object for returning light.
Step 3: Second lens traversal gives v=(10×25)/(25−10)=50/3 cm to the left.
Why: The mirror changes propagation direction, so the second lens object is on the right.
Why not the others: (A) stops at first lens; (C) stops at mirror image; (D) reverses final side.
Key point: Recalculate object and incident side after each optical element.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Threshold frequency from two stopping potentials
questions.question: Stopping potentials for light frequencies f and 2f are 1 V and 3 V for one metal. What is its threshold frequency in terms of f?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) f/2.
Given: eV₁=hf−φ=e(1 V); eV₂=2hf−φ=e(3 V).
Formula/Principle: Subtract equations to eliminate work function: hf=e(2 V).
Step 1: φ=hf−e(1 V)=e(1 V)=hf/2.
Step 2: Threshold f₀=φ/h=f/2.
Why: The difference in stopping potentials measures the energy increase from doubling frequency.
Why not the others: (B) uses the 3 V alone; (C) neglects nonzero kinetic energy at f; (D) places threshold above light already emitting electrons.
Key point: Eliminate φ with two measurements.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In hydrogen, what is wavelength ratio λ(3→2)/λ(2→1) for emitted photons? Use Eₙ=−13.6/n² eV.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 27/5.
Given: Energy gaps are 13.6(1/4−1/9)=13.6×5/36 and 13.6(1−1/4)=13.6×3/4.
Formula/Principle: Photon λ=hc/ΔE; wavelength ratio is inverse gap ratio.
Step 1: λ32/λ21=ΔE21/ΔE32.
Step 2: (3/4)/(5/36)=27/5.
Why: The 3→2 transition has a smaller energy gap and hence longer wavelength.
Why not the others: (A) reverses ratio; (B) and (C) use only part of the level fractions.
Key point: Compute energy gaps before taking inverse wavelength ratios.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A loop lies in the page. Magnetic flux into the page increases. Viewed facing the page, what is the induced conventional current direction?
options: D) No current because field direction is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Counterclockwise, producing outward field.
Why: The induced effect opposes the *increase* of inward flux, requiring an outward magnetic field. Right-hand fingers curling counterclockwise give a thumb pointing out of the page. Fixed field direction does not mean fixed flux when magnitude changes.
Why not the others: (A) Reinforces the increase. (B) Clockwise current produces inward field. (D) Ignores changing magnitude.
Key point: Determine the opposed flux change before using the right-hand rule.
